title: University of Maryland - CS13

question.stem: Select the 4 findings that are most concerning.

options.text: Awakening at night with shortness of breath

question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Heart Failure” medical-surgical faculty case study (Lisa Seldomridge, PhD, RN, CNE; Jennifer Hart, DNP, FNP-BC; Molly Dale, DNP, FNP-BC; Salisbury University, January 25, 2023). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.explanation:
The client is showing signs of worsening heart failure (HF). Crackles in the lung bases, waking at night short of breath, and weight gain are associated with left-sided HF; lower-extremity edema is associated with right-sided HF but is still a concern.
Anxiety, appetite (reported as normal), and frequent urination are not priority concerns compared with the signs of worsening HF, and the heart rate is only slightly elevated.

tabs.title: Clinic Notes
tabs.content:
Day 1 1000:68-year-old male client presents for a routine clinic appointment. Reports “tiring easily when out shopping or for walks”; has been staying home reading and watching television. Reports difficulty sleeping and wakes with shortness of breath in the middle of the night. Reports an 8-lb (3.6-kg) weight gain over the past 2 weeks since the last appointment. States normal appetite. Denies chest pain and back pain. States he is “anxious” about his condition. No known allergies. Current medications: enalapril 20 mg PO twice a day, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg PO twice a day, digoxin 0.125 mg PO once a day.
Assessment: alert and oriented × 4, appears slightly anxious; HR regular at 102; 4+ pitting pedal and pretibial edema; respirations unlabored, crackles in bases bilaterally; abdomen soft, nontender, bowel sounds active; skin warm, dry, and intact; frequent urination of small amounts of clear yellow urine.

question.stem: Select the 2 problems the client is at most risk for developing.
question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Heart Failure” medical-surgical faculty case study (Lisa Seldomridge, PhD, RN, CNE; Jennifer Hart, DNP, FNP-BC; Molly Dale, DNP, FNP-BC; Salisbury University, January 25, 2023). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.explanation:
The client has worsening heart failure and is at risk for fluid volume overload and for electrolyte imbalances from hemodilution. He also takes hydrochlorothiazide and may become hypokalemic if his diet does not include enough potassium.
He is at no or low risk for hyperkalemia, dehydration, anemia, heart attack, diabetes mellitus, and thrombophlebitis.

question.stem: Which abnormal laboratory finding should the nurse address first?
question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Heart Failure” medical-surgical faculty case study (Lisa Seldomridge, PhD, RN, CNE; Jennifer Hart, DNP, FNP-BC; Molly Dale, DNP, FNP-BC; Salisbury University, January 25, 2023). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
The serum potassium must be addressed first: it is dangerously low and can precipitate digoxin toxicity.
The cholesterol is high but is not an urgent issue, and the hematocrit is slightly low, partly from hemodilution. The creatinine is slightly elevated, which bears watching but is not an urgent concern compared with the potassium level.

leftContent.intro: The nurse cares for a 68-year-old male client who presents for a routine clinic appointment.

question.stem: What should the nurse include in the teaching plan for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Increase intake of oral fluids to stay hydrated.
Weigh yourself every day at the same time and in the same clothes.
Limit sodium in the diet to no more than 2 grams per day.
Immediately report a 1-lb (0.5-kg) weight gain in 1 day or 3 lb (1.4 kg) in 1 week.
Take prescribed medication every day, even if feeling better.

question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Heart Failure” medical-surgical faculty case study (Lisa Seldomridge, PhD, RN, CNE; Jennifer Hart, DNP, FNP-BC; Molly Dale, DNP, FNP-BC; Salisbury University, January 25, 2023). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.explanation:
The client is having an exacerbation of heart failure and must be taught self-care: daily weights at the same time in the same clothes, limiting dietary sodium, adding potassium-rich foods, and taking medication as prescribed.
Increasing fluids would worsen the fluid overload. The usual teaching is to report a gain of 2–3 lb (1–1.5 kg) in a day or 5 lb (2.3 kg) in a week. Regular, tolerated activity is encouraged rather than limited.

leftContent.intro: The nurse cares for a 68-year-old male client who presents for a routine clinic appointment.

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take in response to the change in the medical orders? Select all that apply.

options.text: Instruct client to start the new medication today
Tell client to take an additional dose of diuretic today
Request that the provider order a potassium supplement
Ask the dietitian to meet with the client
Determine if the client owns a scale

question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Heart Failure” medical-surgical faculty case study (Lisa Seldomridge, PhD, RN, CNE; Jennifer Hart, DNP, FNP-BC; Molly Dale, DNP, FNP-BC; Salisbury University, January 25, 2023). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Clinic Notes from Day 1 1030.
question.explanation:
The new order for sacubitril/valsartan should be questioned because the client is already taking enalapril: an ACE inhibitor must be stopped at least 36 hours before sacubitril/valsartan is started, because the combination can cause angioedema. The client needs education about stopping digoxin, a potassium supplement for the low potassium, a dietitian consultation about the fluid restriction and potassium-rich foods, and a scale for daily weights.
The client should not start the new medication until the order is clarified, and an extra diuretic dose is not ordered and would worsen the hypokalemia.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify if the finding indicates that the client’s status has improved, worsened, or is unchanged from his condition at the clinic visit 2 weeks earlier.

rows.text: Getting up at night to urinate

question.footnote: Taken from the Maryland Next Gen NCLEX Test Bank Project, University of Maryland School of Nursing: “Heart Failure” medical-surgical faculty case study (Lisa Seldomridge, PhD, RN, CNE; Jennifer Hart, DNP, FNP-BC; Molly Dale, DNP, FNP-BC; Salisbury University, January 25, 2023). Available at https://www.nursing.umaryland.edu/mnwc/initiatives/nextgen-nclex/nextgen-nclex-library/ (Faculty Case Studies). Laboratory values shown in SI units.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Clinic Notes from Day 14 0830. On day 14, the nurse follows up with the client.
question.explanation:
A nagging cough, difficulty catching his breath, sleeping in a recliner (orthopnea), and pink-tinged sputum are signs of worsening left-sided HF that require immediate intervention. Lack of appetite and getting up at night to urinate also show that the heart failure is worsening.
The pulse is slightly improved (102 to 90) and within normal limits. Thirst is not related to the heart failure and is keyed as unchanged.

Day 14 0830:Client called the clinic to report a nagging cough, pink-tinged sputum, and difficulty “catching” his breath. States he is sleeping in a recliner because he cannot breathe when lying down in bed. His wife checked his pulse and it is 90. Reports lack of appetite, thirst, and getting up twice a night to urinate. States he is “worried” about his health. Advised client that worsening symptoms need immediate attention. Spoke with client’s wife, who agreed to take him to the emergency department.
